title: The Night Humanity Moved an Asteroid
excerpt: Four years ago tonight, a spacecraft the size of a vending machine flew itself into a 160-meter asteroid at six kilometers per second while the world watched, one frame per second. DART shortened Dimorphos's orbit by 33 minutes, 27 times the bar for success, and ESA's Hera arrives at the crash site within weeks to inspect the damage.
content:
At 7:14 p.m. Eastern on September 26, 2022, a room full of engineers at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory in Maryland watched a gray, boulder-covered landscape swell to fill a screen, and then the screen went red. “Loss of signal” flashed up. Mission systems engineer Elena Adams jumped out of her seat, threw her arms in the air, and shouted the only words the night required. “We have impact!”

Eleven million kilometers away, the Double Asteroid Redirection Test spacecraft had just ceased to exist. DART, a 570-kilogram box roughly the size of a vending machine, had flown itself into Dimorphos, a 160-meter moonlet orbiting the larger asteroid Didymos, at just over 22,000 kilometers per hour. Nothing about the collision was an accident. It was the whole point of a $325 million mission, the first time in history that humans deliberately hit a celestial body to change how it moves.

Neither asteroid posed any threat to Earth, before the test or after it. That was precisely why the pair was chosen. Didymos and Dimorphos form a binary system, which means the moonlet’s 11-hour, 55-minute orbit around its parent could be measured from ground telescopes by timing the dips in brightness as one body passed in front of the other. Hit the moonlet, shorten the orbit, measure the difference. A planetary deflection experiment with a built-in ruler, run at a safe distance from the only planet anyone cares about.

The spacecraft had left Earth ten months earlier, on November 24, 2021 at 06:21 UTC, riding a Falcon 9 out of Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg (launch 2021-110). Tucked aboard was a hitchhiker, the Italian Space Agency’s LICIACube, a briefcase-sized CubeSat whose job was to survive the evening and photograph what DART could not. The cruise was quiet. The last day was anything but.

T-4 hours

SMART Nav takes the controls

At 19:14 UTC the spacecraft goes fully autonomous. DRACO locks onto Didymos; Dimorphos is still too small and dim to register.

T-1 hour

Dimorphos appears

The moonlet shows up in DRACO's frames as a smudge barely more than a pixel wide, the first close look anyone has ever had.

T-50 minutes

The aimpoint shifts

SMART Nav begins walking its targeting solution from Didymos to Dimorphos as the smaller body brightens.

T-20 minutes

Precision lock

The algorithm drops Didymos entirely and steers on Dimorphos alone. Ground operators can only watch.

T-2.5 minutes

Final maneuver complete

Thrusting ends and DART coasts, streaming one image per second all the way in.

23:14 UTC

Impact

DART strikes within 17 meters of Dimorphos's center at roughly 6.1 km/s. Loss of signal confirms success.

T+2 min 45 s

LICIACube flies through the aftermath

The Italian CubeSat passes about 57 km from Dimorphos and photographs a plume of debris erupting from the surface.

An Algorithm With One Shot

The hardest problem of the night was not hitting an asteroid. It was hitting the right one. Until the final hour, Dimorphos had never been resolved by any telescope or spacecraft. It existed only as a periodic flicker in light curves. DART had to find a target nobody had ever seen, discriminate it from a parent body 25 times brighter sitting almost on top of it, and steer into it at six kilometers per second. No human could fly that intercept. Round-trip light delay to the Didymos system was over a minute, an eternity against terminal-guidance timescales.

So APL gave the job to software. SMART Nav, short for Small-body Maneuvering Autonomous Real-Time Navigation, took over the spacecraft four hours out, processing images from the onboard DRACO camera and issuing its own thruster commands. The engineers who built it drew on decades of missile-guidance heritage from APL’s defense work, adapted for a target that fights back only with physics. For the first three of those four hours, SMART Nav could steer only on Didymos, because Dimorphos was too faint to detect. The target handover was the part of the sequence the team had worried over for years. If the algorithm misjudged which blob of pixels was which, DART would sail harmlessly past, and the mission’s one bullet would be spent.

About an hour before impact, Dimorphos finally registered in DRACO’s images as little more than a single pixel. At 50 minutes out, SMART Nav began sliding its aimpoint toward the moonlet. At 20 minutes, it entered precision lock and ignored Didymos completely. In mission control, engineers stood at consoles they could no longer meaningfully use. The contingency plans, branch decisions, and abort criteria they had rehearsed all summer expired one by one as the range closed. In the last minutes the spacecraft stopped maneuvering entirely and simply fell toward the point the software had chosen.

It chose well. Post-impact reconstruction showed DART struck within 17 meters of Dimorphos’s center, an essentially perfect hit on a body the size of a football stadium, aimed by a machine that had first laid eyes on its target an hour earlier.

Watching a Spacecraft Die in Real Time

What made the evening a global event rather than an engineering milestone was DRACO’s live feed. One image per second, streamed straight to NASA TV. Viewers watched Didymos grow from a point of light into a lumpy diamond, watched Dimorphos detach from its glare and sharpen into an egg-shaped pile of rock, and then watched the surface rush up. The last complete frame, taken two seconds before impact from about 12 kilometers out, showed a patch of ground 31 meters across, strewn with boulders in crisp detail. The final frame arrived as a sliver. The spacecraft was destroyed while the image was still transmitting.

Adams delivered the line of the night at the post-impact press conference, and it has aged well.

As far as we can tell, our first planetary defense test was a success. I think Earthlings should sleep better. Definitely I will.

Three minutes behind DART came the witness. LICIACube, released from the spacecraft fifteen days earlier, tore past Dimorphos at a closest approach of about 57 kilometers and pivoted its two cameras, LEIA and LUKE, at the impact site. Its photos, downlinked over the following days on the CubeSat’s small antenna, showed something nobody had fully anticipated. Dimorphos was wrapped in a bright, expanding cloud of debris, with filaments and streamers of ejecta radiating from the impact point like a firework caught mid-burst. The little Italian spacecraft, ASI’s first deep-space mission, had captured the exact phenomenon that would turn a good result into a spectacular one.

The Ruler Comes Out

Success had a number attached to it before launch. If DART changed Dimorphos’s orbital period by at least 73 seconds, the test would count as a win. That figure was chosen because it was comfortably measurable from Earth, and most pre-impact modeling suggested the change would come in somewhere around ten minutes, give or take a wide error bar that depended on what Dimorphos was actually made of.

For two weeks, telescopes in Chile, South Africa, and elsewhere timed the mutual eclipses of the two asteroids while planetary radar at Goldstone and Green Bank pinged the system directly. On October 11, 2022, NASA Administrator Bill Nelson stood up in Washington and announced the answer. Dimorphos’s orbit had shortened from 11 hours 55 minutes to 11 hours 23 minutes, a change of 32 minutes, plus or minus two. Later refinement in Nature settled on 33.0 minutes. “This is a watershed moment for planetary defense and all of humanity,” Nelson said.

33

Minutes cut from Dimorphos's orbital period

The mission's formal success threshold was 73 seconds. DART beat it by a factor of 27.

The margin demanded an explanation, because a 570-kilogram spacecraft alone could not do that to a body of roughly five billion kilograms. The explanation was sitting in LICIACube’s photos and in ground images like the one atop this article. Two nights after impact, the SOAR telescope in Chile photographed a comet-like trail of debris streaming more than 10,000 kilometers behind Didymos, pushed out by sunlight pressure. The impact had excavated over a million kilograms of rock, and all of that mass leaving Dimorphos at speed acted like exhaust from a rocket engine, pushing back on the asteroid far harder than the spacecraft’s own momentum did.

Physicists bundle that effect into a number called the momentum enhancement factor, beta. A beta of 1 means the target only absorbed the impactor’s momentum. The Nature analysis led by APL’s Andy Cheng found DART’s beta was about 3.6, with a plausible range of 2.2 to 4.9 depending on Dimorphos’s true mass. The recoil from flying ejecta delivered roughly three times more push than the spacecraft itself. For anyone who might someday need to deflect a real threat, that is enormously good news. Loose rubble-pile asteroids, which appear to be common, multiply your effort.

The Debris Kept Talking

The ejecta story did not end in 2022. In December of that year, the Hubble Space Telescope stared at the system long enough to pick out individual objects crawling away from Dimorphos, and in July 2023 David Jewitt’s team published the census. Thirty-seven boulders, ranging from one meter to nearly seven meters across, drifting from the asteroid at around a kilometer per hour, collectively about 0.1 percent of Dimorphos’s mass. “This is a spectacular observation, much better than I expected,” Jewitt said. They were among the faintest objects Hubble has ever measured in the solar system, a slow-motion swarm of house-sized rocks shaken or thrown loose by the impact.

The boulders carry a practical lesson. A kinetic impactor partially disassembles its target while deflecting it. Modeling published in 2024 suggested DART may not have left a conventional crater at all. Dimorphos is so loosely bound that the impact likely reshaped the entire body, slumping it into a new form and shedding material globally. If a future deflection ever happens for real, mission planners will need to account for a debris field, not just a deflected rock. For a 160-meter body none of the fragments threaten anything, but the physics scales.

Nancy Chabot, DART’s coordination lead at APL, spent the victory lap reminding everyone what the result did and did not prove. The impact changed Dimorphos’s speed by a few millimeters per second, she noted, which added up to 33 minutes only because the change compounds every orbit. “Warning time is really key here in order to enable this sort of asteroid deflection,” she said. Kinetic impactors are a tool for threats found years or decades out, which is exactly why the survey telescopes and catalogs matter as much as the interceptor.

Hera Arrives to Inspect the Damage

Which brings the story to this month, because the DART anniversary is no longer just a memory. The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft, launched on October 7, 2024 on a Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral (launch 2024-180), is in the final weeks of its cruise to the crime scene. After a Mars flyby in March 2025 and a deep-space maneuver earlier this year that lined up its orbital plane with the Didymos system, Hera begins a series of precision braking burns in October and arrives at the binary in November 2026, easing into orbit around the pair through a sequence of capture maneuvers in the weeks that follow.

Hera is the accident investigator DART never had. It carries two CubeSats of its own, Juventas and Milani. Juventas will perform the first radar sounding of an asteroid’s interior and eventually attempt to set down on Dimorphos’s surface, while Milani maps the composition of the dust still clinging to the system. The mothership will weigh Dimorphos directly, settle the crater-versus-reshaping question by imaging the impact site, and pin down the asteroid’s mass well enough to collapse that 2.2-to-4.9 beta range into a single useful number. Only then does the DART experiment produce its final answer, the calibrated physics that would let engineers size a deflection mission against a real threat with confidence instead of educated guessing.

Four years ago tonight, an algorithm found a rock no one had ever seen and put a spacecraft into it 17 meters from dead center, and the debris did the rest. It remains the only time our species has measurably rearranged the solar system on purpose. The follow-up inspector is weeks from the scene, and the vending machine’s crater, or whatever is left where it should have been, is about to get its first visitor.
